title: NATURAL JOIN: mechanics and risks
objective: Understand that NATURAL JOIN joins on every same-named column, predict when that silently adds (or removes) join conditions, and replace it with explicit ON or USING.
context: A colleague's notebook uses NATURAL JOIN everywhere because it's short. It worked last month. Then someone added a `region` column to a summary table, and a customer report lost two customers without any error. This lesson shows exactly how that happens.

exercises.title: Line counts per status with NATURAL JOIN
exercises.question: Operations wants the number of order lines per order status.
exercises.prompt: Using NATURAL JOIN (or an equivalent explicit join), return order_status and line_count (number of order_items lines) per status.
hints: orders and order_items share exactly one column name. Which?
FROM orders NATURAL JOIN order_items, then GROUP BY order_status.
SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS line_count FROM orders NATURAL JOIN order_items GROUP BY order_status;
exercises.why: NATURAL JOIN is safe only when you have verified the shared names. Doing that check explicitly is the habit that protects you when it isn't safe.

recall.q: NATURAL JOIN joins on which columns?
recall.a: Every column name the two inputs have in common.

exercises.join_notes: Shared names: only order_id, so NATURAL JOIN = JOIN USING (order_id). Each of 150 lines matches exactly one order → 150 rows, grouped into 5 statuses. Order 60 (pending, no lines) drops out as in any inner join, so 'pending' only counts order 59's lines. No NULLs appear.

exercises.title: Rewrite with USING
exercises.question: Procurement wants each product with its supplier's name and country.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, supplier_name and country for products whose supplier exists, joining with JOIN … USING (supplier_id).
hints: USING takes the shared column name in parentheses.
SELECT product_id, product_name, supplier_name, country FROM products JOIN suppliers USING (supplier_id);
exercises.why: USING is NATURAL JOIN's honest sibling: just as short, but the key is written down, so adding a column to either table can't change the join.

recall.q: How is JOIN … USING (k) different from NATURAL JOIN?
recall.a: USING joins only on the listed column(s); NATURAL joins on all same-named columns.

exercises.join_notes: supplier_id is unique in suppliers: no multiplication. 25 products → 23 rows: product 21 (supplier_id 9, nonexistent) and product 22 (NULL supplier_id) find no supplier and drop. Here NATURAL JOIN would give the same 23 rows, because supplier_id is the only shared name — today.

exercises.title: No shared columns = cross join
exercises.question: An analyst NATURAL JOINed suppliers to categories 'to see which supplier serves which category' and got a suspiciously big result. Quantify it.
exercises.prompt: Return a single row with columns supplier_rows (COUNT of suppliers), category_rows (COUNT of categories) and natural_rows (COUNT(*) of suppliers NATURAL JOIN categories).
hints: Three scalar subqueries in one SELECT.
Compare the column lists: do suppliers and categories share any name?
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM suppliers) AS supplier_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM categories) AS category_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM suppliers NATURAL JOIN categories) AS natural_rows;
exercises.why: With no common column, NATURAL JOIN raises no error — it returns the cartesian product. On real tables that's billions of rows and a very expensive mistake.

recall.q: What does NATURAL JOIN do when the tables share no column names?

exercises.join_notes: suppliers (supplier_id, supplier_name, country) and categories (category_id, category_name, parent_category_id) share no column name, so the NATURAL JOIN has no condition at all: 5 × 14 = 70 rows, every supplier paired with every category. Nothing is NULL and nothing is missing — it's all noise. There is no real key between these tables; the relationship goes through products.

exercises.title: The extra shared column: region
exercises.question: A customer report joins customers to a pre-built order-count table. The pre-built table carries region too, and the report is missing customers. Build it correctly.
exercises.prompt: First build order_counts AS (SELECT o.customer_id, c.region, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders o JOIN customers c USING (customer_id) GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.region). Then join customers to order_counts on customer_id ONLY and return customer_id, name, region (from customers) and order_count for every customer that has orders.
hints: Write the CTE exactly as given, then join it to customers.
customers NATURAL JOIN order_counts would join on customer_id AND region. What happens to customers with a NULL region?
... FROM customers c JOIN order_counts oc USING (customer_id) — and select c.region (qualified, because both sides have region).
exercises.why: Denormalised summary tables often repeat descriptive columns (region, name, segment). With NATURAL JOIN each such column becomes a hidden join condition.

recall.q: Why does NATURAL JOIN on (customer_id, region) drop customers with a NULL region?
recall.a: Because NULL = NULL is not true, so the extra region condition fails for them.

exercises.join_notes: order_counts has 17 rows (one per customer with orders; orphan customer 99 is already gone because the CTE inner-joins customers). Joining USING (customer_id) returns all 17. `customers NATURAL JOIN order_counts` returns only 15: it also requires customers.region = order_counts.region, and for customers 9 (David Kim) and 16 (Ava Thompson) both regions are NULL, so NULL = NULL fails — no error, two customers silently missing.

exercises.title: The extra shared column: name
exercises.question: An analyst joined a product-sales summary to a product-supplier lookup with NATURAL JOIN and got an empty report. Both summaries use a column called `name`.
exercises.prompt: Build sales AS (SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name AS name, SUM(i.quantity) AS units_sold FROM products p JOIN order_items i USING (product_id) GROUP BY p.product_id) and supplier_lookup AS (SELECT p.product_id, s.supplier_name AS name FROM products p JOIN suppliers s USING (supplier_id)). Join them on product_id only and return product_id, product_name, supplier_name and units_sold.
hints: Both CTEs have product_id AND name. NATURAL JOIN would require the product name to equal the supplier name.
Join with USING (product_id) and disambiguate the two `name` columns with aliases.
SELECT product_id, sa.name AS product_name, sl.name AS supplier_name, sa.units_sold FROM sales sa JOIN supplier_lookup sl USING (product_id);
exercises.why: Generic column names (name, id, status, value, n) are everywhere in staging layers. NATURAL JOIN turns every such collision into a silent filter.

recall.q: Why did the NATURAL JOIN return 0 rows?
recall.a: It also joined on `name`, and no product name equals a supplier name.

exercises.join_notes: sales has 22 rows (products that sold) and supplier_lookup 23 (products with an existing supplier); both are one row per product, so no multiplication. USING (product_id) returns 20 rows: product 21 and 22 sold but have no valid supplier, and products 23-25 have a supplier but never sold. sales NATURAL JOIN supplier_lookup returns 0 rows — it adds `sales.name = supplier_lookup.name`, i.e. product name = supplier name.

exercises.title: Generic aliases collide: n and n
exercises.question: Growth compares each customer's valid orders with their tracked purchase events. Both pre-aggregated tables call their count `n`.
exercises.prompt: Pre-aggregate valid orders per customer (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) as (customer_id, n) and purchase web events per customer (event_type = 'purchase') as (customer_id, n). Join them on customer_id only and return customer_id, valid_orders and purchase_events for customers present in both.
hints: Two GROUP BY customer_id subqueries/CTEs, each with a COUNT(*) AS n.
NATURAL JOIN would match on customer_id AND n — keeping only customers whose two counts happen to be equal. Use USING (customer_id).
SELECT customer_id, vo.n AS valid_orders, pe.n AS purchase_events FROM vo JOIN pe USING (customer_id);
exercises.why: This bug is especially nasty because the result is not empty — it's a plausible-looking subset (only customers whose metrics coincide), so nobody notices.

recall.q: Which customers survive vo NATURAL JOIN pe?
recall.a: Only those whose valid-order count equals their purchase-event count.

exercises.join_notes: vo has one row per customer_id with a valid order (17 ids, including orphan 99) and pe one row per customer with a purchase event (12), so the join is one-to-one on customer_id: 11 customers appear in both → 11 rows. The NATURAL JOIN version returns only 2 rows — customers 9 (2 and 2) and 13 (1 and 1) — because it also requires vo.n = pe.n. Pre-aggregating also avoided the orders × events fan-out of Lesson 16.

worked_example.question: What does NATURAL JOIN do between orders and order_items?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT order_id, order_status, product_id, quantity
FROM orders
NATURAL JOIN order_items
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: The only shared column name is order_id, so this equals `JOIN order_items USING (order_id)`: 150 rows (order 60 has no items and drops, as with any inner join). Note `order_id` is written unqualified — NATURAL/USING merge the shared column into one.

recipe:
**Recipe: read (and replace) a NATURAL JOIN in 4 moves**

1. **List the columns of both inputs** and find every name they share. NATURAL JOIN = INNER JOIN
   with `ON a.c1 = b.c1 AND a.c2 = b.c2 …` for *all* shared names.
2. **Zero shared names** → it silently becomes a CROSS JOIN (every row × every row).
3. **An extra shared name** (`region`, `name`, `status`, `updated_at`, a generic `n`) → an extra
   equality condition: rows where those differ — or are NULL — vanish.
4. Rewrite explicitly: `JOIN … USING (customer_id)` (shared column output once, no alias needed) or
   `JOIN … ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id` (most explicit; works when names differ).

```sql
-- risky: joins on customer_id AND region (if both sides have region)
SELECT * FROM customers NATURAL JOIN order_counts;
-- explicit:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.region, oc.order_count
FROM customers AS c
JOIN order_counts AS oc USING (customer_id);
```

**USING vs ON:** `USING (k)` requires the same name on both sides and outputs one `k` column;
`ON a.k = b.k` keeps both. Other same-named columns are NOT joined by USING — but you must qualify them
(`c.region`) to avoid ambiguity.

**Rule of thumb for production SQL:** never NATURAL JOIN. Your query's meaning should not change when
someone adds a column to a table. Snowflake supports NATURAL JOIN and USING with identical semantics.
common_mistakes: Assuming NATURAL JOIN uses 'the obvious key' — it uses every same-named column.
Not noticing that zero shared columns turns NATURAL JOIN into a CROSS JOIN.
Forgetting that an extra shared nullable column drops rows where it is NULL on both sides.
Giving pre-aggregated columns generic names (n, name, value) and then joining NATURALly.
With USING, selecting an unqualified column that exists on both sides but isn't in USING (e.g. region) — ambiguous.
recall: What three outcomes can an unexpected shared column name cause in NATURAL JOIN?
Dropped rows (values differ or are NULL), an empty result, or — with no shared names — a cross join.
What's the safe short alternative to NATURAL JOIN?
Why is NATURAL JOIN dangerous in production code?
Its join condition changes silently whenever a column is added or renamed.
